sections.text: # Surficial Geology — Glacial, Fluvial, Karst, Coastal, Pedogenesis

metadata.title: Surficial Geology - Glacial, Fluvial, Karst, Coastal, Pedogenesis

sections.text: **Bridge — surficial geology as the rendering layer over tectonic infrastructure:** Plate tectonics is the backend: it sets topographic relief, rock type distribution, and the substrate. Surficial processes are the rendering layer: ice, water, wind, and gravity continuously reshape the interface that humans actually experience. The backend creates the raw geometry (mountains via collision, valleys via rifting); the frontend optimizes it toward equilibrium (erosion reducing relief, deposition filling basins). This is full-stack geology — the backend processes operate on 10⁶–10⁸ year timescales; surficial processes render on 10²–10⁵ year timescales, fast enough to be observable in a human lifetime. Climate is the runtime environment that determines which surficial processes dominate: glacial at high latitude/altitude, fluvial in temperate zones, eolian in arid zones, chemical (karst) where carbonate rock and rainfall intersect. Change the climate, change the active process set — but the tectonic substrate persists.

sections.text: ## The Big Picture

metadata.title: Surficial Geology - Glacial, Fluvial, Karst, Coastal, Pedogenesis

sections.text: Surficial geology covers processes that shape Earth's surface by moving material without involving plate tectonics directly. The agents — ice, water, wind, gravity — operate at human-perceivable timescales and produce the landscapes we actually live in.

metadata.title: Surficial Geology - Glacial, Fluvial, Karst, Coastal, Pedogenesis

sections.text:
**Glacial erosion mechanisms:**
- **Abrasion** — rock fragments frozen in ice grind bedrock (striations + polish)
- **Plucking/quarrying** — ice freezes to bedrock, pulls away blocks on downstream side
- **Meltwater** — subglacial streams erode channels (P-forms, Nye channels)

sections.text: **Till vs outwash** — Till is unsorted, unstratified debris deposited directly by ice (diamicton). Outwash is sorted, stratified sand/gravel deposited by meltwater streams (stratified drift). Outwash plains = sandur (Iceland term).

sections.text: Clay paradox: very fine clay is harder to erode than sand because clay particles cohere (electrostatic forces). Once in suspension, clay stays suspended at very low velocities.

metadata.title: Surficial Geology - Glacial, Fluvial, Karst, Coastal, Pedogenesis

sections.text:
**Meander mechanics:**
- Thalweg (fastest flow) hits outer bank → erosion → undercut cliff (cut bank)
- Inner bank = deposition → point bar
- Over time, meander loop tightens → oxbow lake when cut off
- Meander wavelength ≈ 10–14× channel width (independent of scale)

sections.text: Karst develops where carbonate (limestone, dolomite) or evaporite (gypsum) rock is dissolved by slightly acidic groundwater:

```
DISSOLUTION REACTION:
CaCO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → Ca²⁺ + 2HCO₃⁻

sections.text:
(Rainwater absorbs CO₂ → carbonic acid; dissolves limestone;
 Ca²⁺ + HCO₃⁻ carried away in solution)

sections.text:
SURFACE FEATURES:
Sinkhole (doline): depression from collapse/dissolution
Polje: large flat-floored depression
Karren: small-scale grooves on bare limestone surface
Disappearing streams: surface water enters underground at swallet

metadata.title: Surficial Geology - Glacial, Fluvial, Karst, Coastal, Pedogenesis

sections.text:
SUBSURFACE FEATURES:
Caves (speleological system)
Stalactites: hang from ceiling (drip water)
Stalagmites: grow from floor up
Columns: where they meet
Flowstone: sheet deposit on cave floor/walls
```

metadata.title: Surficial Geology - Glacial, Fluvial, Karst, Coastal, Pedogenesis

sections.text: **Sinkhole hazard** — Cover-collapse sinkholes: dissolution of limestone under a cover of sand/clay. No surface warning until roof collapse. Common in Florida, central Texas, Yucatan.

metadata.title: Surficial Geology - Glacial, Fluvial, Karst, Coastal, Pedogenesis

sections.text: **Karst aquifer** — Very productive but also vulnerable: rapid water movement through conduit networks means little filtering → pollution travels fast.

sections.text: ### Loess — Wind-Deposited Silt

metadata.title: Surficial Geology - Glacial, Fluvial, Karst, Coastal, Pedogenesis

sections.text: Loess is glacially-ground silt (rock flour) transported by wind and deposited as thick, unstratified blankets:

metadata.title: Surficial Geology - Glacial, Fluvial, Karst, Coastal, Pedogenesis

sections.text:
```
PROPERTIES:
  Grain size: 20–50 μm (silt; too fine for dune, too coarse for dust)
  Structure: vertical jointing; stands in near-vertical bluffs
  Composition: quartz + feldspar + carbonates (not heavily weathered)
  Thickness: up to 300m (Loess Plateau, China)

metadata.title: Surficial Geology - Glacial, Fluvial, Karst, Coastal, Pedogenesis

sections.text:
GLOBAL DISTRIBUTION:
  China Loess Plateau: 640,000 km²; 100–300m thick; source = Gobi Desert
  US Great Plains: source = Pleistocene outwash from ice sheets
  Pampas (Argentina): Southern Hemisphere equivalent
  Rhine Valley, Ukraine: European loess from periglacial outwash

metadata.title: Surficial Geology - Glacial, Fluvial, Karst, Coastal, Pedogenesis

sections.text:
AGRICULTURAL SIGNIFICANCE:
  Among most fertile soils on Earth (Mollisols developed on loess)
  US Midwest, Ukraine, North China = breadbaskets built on loess
  High porosity + vertical jointing = excellent water retention
  Vulnerability: gully erosion when disturbed (vertical jointing means
  slopes fail suddenly along joint planes)
```

sections.text: ## Pedogenesis — Soil Formation

metadata.title: Surficial Geology - Glacial, Fluvial, Karst, Coastal, Pedogenesis

sections.text: Soil = weathered regolith + organic matter + organisms. The O-A-B-C horizon sequence:

metadata.title: Surficial Geology - Glacial, Fluvial, Karst, Coastal, Pedogenesis

sections.text:
```
HORIZON  NAME           DESCRIPTION
-------  -------------  ----------------------------------------
O        Organic        Litter, humus (only in forested soils)
A        Topsoil        Mixed mineral + organic; darkest; highest
                        biological activity (root zone)
B        Subsoil        Illuviation (accumulated clays, oxides,
         (illuvial)     carbonates leached from A); iron-rich
C        Parent         Partially weathered bedrock fragments;
         material       little soil structure
R        Bedrock        Unweathered parent rock
```

metadata.title: Surficial Geology - Glacial, Fluvial, Karst, Coastal, Pedogenesis

sections.text: **CLORPT factors** (Jenny 1941) — Soil = f(Climate, Organisms, Relief, Parent material, Time):

metadata.title: Surficial Geology - Glacial, Fluvial, Karst, Coastal, Pedogenesis

sections.text:
| Factor | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| Climate | Temperature + precipitation drive weathering rate and leaching; most important at global scale |
| Organisms | Vegetation type determines organic matter input; earthworms mix; mycorrhizae facilitate |
| Relief (topography) | Slope angle/aspect affects water drainage; north-facing slopes cooler in N hemisphere |
| Parent material | Starting composition; granite vs basalt vs limestone → very different soils |
| Time | More developed profile = older soil |

metadata.title: Surficial Geology - Glacial, Fluvial, Karst, Coastal, Pedogenesis

metadata.title: Surficial Geology - Glacial, Fluvial, Karst, Coastal, Pedogenesis

sections.text:
| Order | Climate/Setting | Key Feature | Agricultural relevance |
|-------|----------------|-------------|----------------------|
| Mollisol | Temperate grassland | Deep, organic, A horizon; base-rich | Most productive (US Midwest, Ukraine) |
| Oxisol | Humid tropical | Deep weathering; Fe/Al oxides; nutrient-poor | Rainforest soils; leached |
| Aridisol | Desert | Evaporite accumulation; caliche layer | Low productivity; irrigation needed |
| Inceptisol | Young soils | Weakly developed; forests, mountains | Moderate |
| Ultisol | Subtropical humid | Leached; red from Fe oxides | SE US; moderate |
| Entisol | Very young | Minimal profile; alluvium, sand | Fertile if fresh alluvium |
| Spodosol | Boreal forest | Bleached E horizon; spodic B | Acidic; conifer forests |

metadata.title: Surficial Geology - Glacial, Fluvial, Karst, Coastal, Pedogenesis

sections.text:
**Slope stability factors:**
- Angle: failure occurs when shear stress (driven by gravity component along slope) exceeds shear strength (cohesion + friction × normal stress)
- Water: raises pore pressure → reduces effective normal stress → reduces friction → reduces shear strength; also adds weight
- Clay minerals: low friction angle (~15°), expand/contract with moisture → plastic failure
- Vegetation: root reinforcement stabilizes slopes; removal (logging, fire) dramatically increases failure probability

metadata.title: Surficial Geology - Glacial, Fluvial, Karst, Coastal, Pedogenesis

sections.text:
**Notable events:**
- Frank Slide (Alberta, 1903): rockslide from Turtle Mountain; 70 million tonnes, 90 dead, 3 km run-out in 100 seconds
- Vargas (Venezuela, 1999): debris flows + mudflows on steep coastal slopes after extreme rainfall; ~30,000 dead
- Oso (Washington, 2014): slow-moving earthflow that accelerated; 43 dead; site had prior movement history

sections.text: ## Decision Cheat Sheet

metadata.title: Surficial Geology - Glacial, Fluvial, Karst, Coastal, Pedogenesis

sections.text:
| Landscape / Hazard Question | Use This Diagnostic | Likely Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Was this valley cut by ice or water? | Cross-section shape + striations + hanging valleys | U-shaped polished valley = glacial; V-shaped channel = fluvial incision |
| Which way did the glacier move? | Striations, roche moutonnee, drumlin long axes | Smooth stoss/rough lee and streamlined hills indicate ice-flow direction |
| Is this till or outwash? | Sorting + stratification | Unsorted diamicton = direct ice deposit; sorted sand/gravel = meltwater deposit |
| Is a river migrating or avulsing? | Cut banks, point bars, oxbows, levees, crevasse splays | Channel geometry records active floodplain evolution |
| Is karst collapse plausible? | Carbonate/evaporite bedrock + closed depressions + disappearing streams | Conduit flow and roof collapse can produce sudden sinkholes |
| What wind regime made the dune field? | Dune shape + sand supply + vegetation | Barchan, transverse, linear, star, and parabolic dunes encode wind directionality |
| Is the slope close to failure? | Material, water, slope angle, weak planes, vegetation loss | Raised pore pressure and reduced root strength can turn slow creep into rapid failure |
| Is the soil young or mature? | Horizon development + CLORPT context | Thick A/B horizons imply time and stability; Entisols/Inceptisols imply youth or disturbance |
| Will the landform preserve in rock record? | Accommodation, burial, reworking risk | Active surface forms matter most geologically when rapidly buried or repeatedly regenerated |
